title: Utah Code Title 13, Chapter 72: Artificial Intelligence Policy Act
author: Utah Legislature

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The statute operationalises the cluster’s selective, risk-based deployment proposition through concrete admission standards: demonstrated technical and financial capacity, consumer benefit-risk balancing, active risk controls, proportionate testing and optional expert consultation. Its endorsement and liability disclaimers further distinguish supervised regulatory participation from validation of the technology.

kp.k: The Act defines AI broadly across applications
kp.d: Section 13-72-101 defines artificial intelligence by its capacity to make predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing environments, and AI technology by its incorporation into systems, applications, or products. These are statutory definitions rather than findings about AI performance or effects on legal work.

kp.k: A dedicated office administers adaptive AI policymaking
kp.d: Section 13-72-201 creates the Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy within the Department of Commerce. Its duties include administering a learning laboratory, consulting businesses and other stakeholders on regulatory proposals, and establishing rules for consumer disclosures, participant reporting, and limited participation extensions. It must report annually before November 30 to the Business and Labor Interim Committee on the learning agenda, findings, participation, outcomes, agreements, and recommended legislation; consumer guidance is discretionary.

kp.k: The laboratory links deployment experiments to regulatory learning
kp.d: Section 13-72-301 establishes a research and analysis program intended to inform the state regulatory framework, encourage responsible AI deployment, evaluate regulatory effectiveness and viability with AI companies, and generate legislative and regulatory recommendations. The office must periodically set a learning agenda and may consult agencies, governmental entities, industry, academic institutions, and other experts. These are statutory purposes, not reported findings that experimentation has succeeded.

kp.k: Mitigation and interpretation agreements provide distinct regulatory mechanisms
kp.d: Sections 13-72-101 and 13-72-401 provide application-based, temporary arrangements involving participants, the office, and relevant agencies or governmental entities. Regulatory mitigation permits AI deployment despite potentially obstructive laws or rules, with cure periods, reduced civil fines, or tailored conditions. Joint interpretation instead clarifies how state law or rules apply to AI technology. The definition of governmental entity includes the judiciary, educational institutions, and political subdivisions; the text does not establish a legal-profession-specific exemption.

kp.k: Agreements require safeguards, bounded deployment, disclosures, and audits
kp.d: Section 13-72-401 requires agreements to specify deployment limits, safeguards, any mitigation granted, required consumer disclosures, and reporting requirements for office audits. Deployment limits may concern user numbers and types, geography, or other implementation constraints. The office must consult relevant agencies and governmental entities on agreement terms and regularly audit participants' application of AI while agreements remain effective.

kp.k: Admission depends on capability, resources, benefits, and risk controls
kp.d: Section 13-72-402 requires participants to demonstrate technical competence for responsible development, implementation, use, or supervision; sufficient financial resources during testing; potential substantial consumer benefits that may outweigh risks from mitigated enforcement; an effective risk-monitoring and minimization plan; and risk-appropriate limits on testing scale, scope, and duration. The office may consult agencies, governmental entities, and outside experts. Potential benefits are eligibility considerations, not established consumer outcomes.

kp.k: Participation preserves legal exposure and permits immediate removal
kp.d: Section 13-72-401 preserves legal and regulatory requirements not expressly waived or modified by mitigation, or clarified through joint interpretation. The office may terminate agreements at any time for any reason, and participants have no expectation of a property right or participation license. Violations of law, regulation, or agreement terms may trigger immediate removal and applicable civil and criminal penalties. Participation is neither state endorsement nor approval, and the statute disclaims state responsibility for claims and losses arising from participation or actions under agreements.

kp.k: Demonstration periods are time-limited with restricted extensions
kp.d: Section 13-72-403 caps an initial demonstration period at 12 months. A participant may request a 12-month extension no later than 30 days before the ongoing period ends. The office must decide before expiration and may grant up to two extensions for either agreement type.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Utah Legislature establishes a conditional route for AI deployment under temporary regulatory mitigation or clarification, rather than predicting changes to legal services.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain statute about AI governance. It provides for agreements that permit deployment despite potentially obstructive laws or rules, or clarify how state law or rules apply to AI. These are statutory mechanisms, not findings that AI has already transformed a market. The chapter makes no concrete prediction about lawyer displacement, legal fees, law-firm structures, or access to justice.

pts.k: The statute treats substantial consumer benefits from AI as a possibility to be demonstrated and makes supervised experimentation a basis for future regulatory recommendations.
pts.d: The Legislature states that the learning laboratory is intended to encourage responsible deployment and investigate AI's risks, benefits, impacts, and policy implications. Eligibility requires a showing of potential consumer benefits that may outweigh identified risks from mitigated enforcement. This is a conditional eligibility proposition and a statement of institutional purpose, not an empirical conclusion that benefits outweigh risks or that the program will succeed.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The basis is statutory authority; the supplied chapter contains no empirical evidence of AI benefits, deployment outcomes, or market effects.
pts.d: The Utah Legislature prescribes a process to generate findings through research, participant reporting, regular audits, and consultation. These prospective evidence-gathering requirements should not be treated as completed studies or demonstrated results. Participation expressly does not constitute state endorsement or approval.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Deployment arrangements are temporary, risk-limited, and revocable: an initial period of up to 12 months can receive up to two 12-month extensions.
pts.d: An extension must be requested no later than 30 days before the ongoing period ends. Applicants must demonstrate technical capability, sufficient financial resources, a risk-monitoring and minimization plan, and appropriately limited testing. Agreements must specify scope, safeguards, any mitigation, consumer disclosures, and audit reporting. Unmodified legal requirements continue to apply, and the office may terminate participation at any time. The supplied text includes a May 1, 2024 effective-date header and section annotations identifying 2026 amendments; it does not separately establish the effective date of those amendments. Annual legislative reporting is due before November 30.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The framework affects AI developers and deployers in Utah, consumers, and public bodies responsible for oversight and policy development.
pts.d: Persons using or proposing to use AI in Utah may apply for agreements but assume eligibility, disclosure, safeguard, and reporting obligations. Consumers are the intended beneficiaries of responsible deployment and receive required disclosures; the office may also publish educational guidance. Relevant agencies and governmental entities participate in agreement design and oversight. The statutory definition of governmental entity includes the judiciary, educational institutions, and political subdivisions, but this does not itself establish changes to legal practice or exemptions from professional regulation.
